transcript:
Meeting Header
Date: 2025-08-14
Time: 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~1h 2m
Attendees: Aaron Patel (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Leo Chen (Redwood Solutions), Jenna Morales (CTO, Ecliptic Health), Mike Yoon (Platform Eng), Priya Nair (Head of Security)

Summary: quick technical deep dive to reconcile performance expectations for dedicated vs hosted, dig into noisy neighbor mitigation, KV cache hit rates, batching windows, and quantization strategy. Customer wants a pilot for throughput guarantees and isolation. Reference: internal benchmark spreadsheet (link shared in chat: https://redwood-internal/sheets/ecliptic-benchmarks) and security packet (link: https://redwood.com/sec/ecliptic-scan)

Topics: runtime perf, SLOs, KV cache, continuous batching, cold-starts, int8 quantization, VPC/private deployment, dedicated capacity sizing, fallback policies

Transcript body:
[00:00] Aaron: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, we're aiming to run through workload characteristics, perf targets, and then outline a pilot. Samira will lead the perf bits. Jenna, mind giving a quick run-down of what Ecliptic is trying to protect against?
[00:18] Jenna: Yeah sure. Uh, main ask — we run clinical summarization pipelines and realtime triage chat. Latency is, like, user-visible for triage so p95 ideally < 350ms for short prompts, and throughput is batch processing for nightly scoring. Also, data is PHI-ish so VPC and KMS is a hard requirement.
[00:35] Mike: Our current infra is GKE public clusters, but we want dedicated inference for compliance and to avoid noisy neighbor spikes we saw when other tenants had huge bursts.
[00:48] Samira: Cool. So the two levers we usually talk about are isolation (dedicated GPU pools) and runtime controls — batching window, prefix / KV cache hit policy. For the triage path, are prompts short? Average tokens?
[01:05] Jenna: For triage the median seq length is around 120 tokens, 95th around 460. Nightly scoring jobs are long — up to 4k tokens.
[01:18] Leo: That distribution matters because it affects KV cache size and memory pressure on the model's KV store and therefore whether we can keep high hit rates. If your 95th is 460, we can still design a cache profile but it changes the batching shapes.
[01:32] Mike: We saw p99 spikes to 3 seconds last month, presumably due to neighbor activity on shared pools.
[01:40] Aaron: Right, noisy neighbor. That's exactly where Dedicated helps — fenced capacity, plus we can reserve burst headroom. But there's always a question of economics. Samira, can you talk numbers — like expected token/sec and latency at different concurrencies on a dedicated pool?
[01:58] Samira: Sure. For reference, our baseline tests on a A100-equivalent dedicated slot with model X-7B quantized to int8, with continuous batching optimized, we saw roughly 150 tokens/sec at concurrency 1 and p95 around 220ms for 128-token sequences; at concurrency 8 with batching window 20ms, that goes to ~1100 tokens/sec total but p95 jumps to ~480ms — so tradeoff. Also note these numbers vary with sequence length.
[02:30] Jenna: When you say batching window 20ms, is that server-imposed? Do we control it per-route?
[02:38] Samira: You can configure per-route batching targets and max delay. We add adaptive limits so latency SLOs are prioritized. Important detail: continuous KV cache improves prefix reuse so many triage prompts hit cache and avoid full context recompute.
[02:53] Mike: How accurate are cache-hit estimates? In our on-prem tests we often saw lower-than-expected hit rates because prefixes vary.
[03:02] Leo: Yeah, that's real. We usually recommend collecting a 72-hour trace and running our hit-rate analyzer (we shared tool link in chat). For Ecliptic, you may have templated prompts so hit rates could be 45-70% for triage. Nightly scoring will have very low prefix reuse so little cache benefit.
[03:25] Priya: Security note — if we go Dedicated in Redwood-hosted but within our VPC peering, what is control-plane visibility? Are logs stored on Redwood or do we push to our SIEM? Need SOC2 artifacts.
[03:37] Aaron: Good question. For Dedicated we can enable customer-managed logging via S3 or push to their SIEM via syslog connectors; audit logs can be exported and key material stays in your KMS when you enable BYOK. We'll share SOC2 report and our security packet after the call.
[03:53] Jenna: How about fallbacks — if dedicated pool hits its quota, can requests spill to hosted shared tier temporarily?
[04:01] Samira: We support configurable fallback policies. You can set a policy like 'fail closed' or 'spill with redaction'. Often customers choose spill to a smaller model variant on hosted with strict logging rules. Note: spill may change latency and output quality; we recommend canarying.
[04:19] Mike: Regarding quantization — you mentioned int8. Any risks for hallucinations or quality drop for our clinical text?
[04:26] Samira: Quantization can slightly change token probabilities, but for many models we have quantization-aware tuning and we've got regen/rescoring flows to catch regressions. We'll do a small eval on your prompt set. If it's problematic, we can keep small critical routes unquantized or use higher-precision kernels.
[04:45] Jenna: Can you also explain kernel selection? We run on AWS G5s and some customers prefer providers with different kernel stacks.
[04:53] Leo: Runtime picks kernels based on model architecture and sequence lengths; we have a compilation step that selects fastest code path and memory layout. On A100 we use cuBLAS/cuDNN fused kernels for attention; on G5e/Trn variants there's alternative kernels. We'll include per-hardware perf tables.
[05:14] Aaron: Let's talk SLOs. You mentioned p95 <350ms earlier. Is that for all triage traffic or only certain priority users?
[05:22] Jenna: Only priority users, about 20% of the traffic. The rest can be a bit higher, p95 < 600ms acceptable.
[05:30] Samira: Fine, so we can set two service classes — 'priority' pinned to reserved instances with tighter batching window and higher cache reservation, and 'standard' on same pool but more tolerant or on a separate pool.
[05:45] Mike: What about autoscaling? Last time we had a cold-start issue where adding nodes took a few minutes.
[05:51] Samira: We have warm standby capacity and can pre-warm kernels; with Dedicated we can keep a minimum reserved capacity so scale-up latency is near-zero for small increments. For large autoscale, we can also route overflow to hosted for immediate capacity.
[06:07] Jenna: What's the expected per-token cost delta between hosted and dedicated? Ballpark.
[06:12] Aaron: Ballpark, dedicated reduces per-token compute cost by ~20-35% depending on commit level; but you pay for reserved capacity. We'll send explicit numbers for your projected throughput.
[06:26] Priya: On the security side we need to confirm KMS integration, hardware-level attestations, and ability to delete logs. Also need to know who has access to key rotation and if Redwood holds any keys by default.
[06:40] Aaron: With BYOK, keys are customer-owned in most options; Redwood never has plaintext access. We'll detail HSM/BYOK options in the security packet.
[06:49] Mike: Can the KV cache be evicted per-tenant? We worry about one job filling cache and harming the triage latency.
[06:57] Samira: Yes, on Dedicated we can enforce tenant cache quotas and background eviction policies. Also you can set per-route cache TTLs.
[07:08] Jenna: For the nightly long jobs, we probably want to schedule them during off-peak and maybe gate them to a separate pool.
[07:14] Leo: Agreed. Separating workloads is the simplest way to avoid interference. We'll show a recommended pool layout: 2 reserved slots for triage (priority), 4 for nightly scoring in a separate pool with burst headroom.
[07:28] Aaron: Let's talk about the pilot. Customer wants throughput guarantees — what's reasonable for a two-node dedicated pilot?
[07:35] Samira: Two A100-equivalent nodes—if you route priority triage across them, you can expect roughly 2 x 1100 tokens/sec at batching tuned, but p95 will depend on concurrency. For strict p95 <350ms on the priority class, I'd recommend reserving a single node per aggressive headroom (i.e., more like 3 nodes) or lower concurrency; we should run the pilot to measure.
[07:56] Jenna: Ok. The pilot should be realistic — run our triage workload and nightly scoring for at least 48 hours. We'll provide sample prompt traces and an approximate token budget.
[08:07] Samira: Perfect. We'll spin up the pilot in a dedicated VPC-peered Dedicated environment. Note on peering — there are some routing constraints, but we support private peering and private control plane.
[08:19] Priya: Any auditing for control-plane actions? We need immutable audit trails for changes to rollout policies and keys.
[08:26] Leo: Yes, we export immutable audit logs with sequence numbers, and support push to your SIEM; we'll annotate who made changes. We'll show sample log lines.
[08:36] Mike: About instrumentation — can we get per-route p50/p95/p99 as well as token-level cost breakdown so we can attribute costs to teams?
[08:44] Aaron: Yes, Redwood Console provides token-level cost, per-route breakdown, and traces. We can also export raw metrics.
[08:52] Jenna: One last quality question — how do you handle hallucination regressions when switching model variants or enabling quantization?
[08:59] Samira: We have eval hooks, reranking, and can auto-run regression suites on any model or quantization change. For clinical text we'll propose a manual review loop for first 1000 items.
[09:12] Aaron: Alright, recap — Redwood will: 1) send dedicated sizing spreadsheet and pricing, 2) schedule a 48-hour dedicated pilot in a VPC-peered environment, 3) run evals on customer's prompt set for int8 quantization safety, 4) provide SOC2 and BYOK docs. Customer will: 1) share prompt traces and sequence-length distribution, 2) confirm token budget for pilot, 3) provide security contact to exchange questionnaire.
[09:34] Jenna: That matches our expectations. Timeline: we'd like the pilot to start the week of 2025-08-25.
[09:42] Samira: We'll target that. Any blockers?
[09:45] Priya: Please send the security questionnaire asap.
[09:48] Aaron: Will do. Thanks everyone.
[09:51] (end)

Notes: occasional transcription errors present: 'K V cash' appears in parts of the transcript export; model name X-7B in notes may be shorthand. Links shared in chat were placeholders. Contact: Aaron.Patel@redwood.com
